segments.speaker: PERFORMER
segments.text: Are you still there? Good. I need you to hear this because the screen is the only one in the room that does not pretend to be innocent. UEC was not built to make life beautiful. It was built because capitalism became too successful at producing things, and that is a problem capitalism never admits until it is standing in the floodwater.

segments.speaker: PERFORMER
segments.text: So the system does what the system always does: it invents a place for excess to go. Excess workers. Excess machines. Excess capital. Excess everything. It calls this coordination. It calls this management. It calls this stability. And because it speaks in clean words, everyone is supposed to clap.

segments.speaker: PERFORMER
segments.text: The paper is the joke, and the joke is serious. Officially, it is a labor slip. Unofficially, any paper will do. A newspaper. A receipt. A blank page. Which means the real object is not the paper at all, but the permission to be folded back into labor. It is the smallest possible monument to a very large system.

segments.speaker: PERFORMER
segments.text: A worker goes in, shows the paper, and the paper says: today you may participate in value production. Not because the paper has value. Because the paper marks the border between your body and the machine that wants your body to become usable again. That is why it matters. Not sentiment. Reproduction.

segments.speaker: PERFORMER
segments.text: And yes, the system is absurd on purpose. It keeps people busy even when there is too much production, too much automation, too much optimization. It does not solve the contradiction. It relocates it. It preserves capital by turning overproduction into a ritual and labor into a ceremony.

segments.speaker: PERFORMER
segments.text: That is why the risk is not just that one factory stops. The risk is that workers stop agreeing to be the solution to capitalism's own mess. Once that happens, the whole reproduction cycle opens up like a fault line. And then the machine does what machines do when the people inside it no longer cooperate: it starts to explain itself. Badly.

segments.speaker: PERFORMER
segments.text: So yes — the paper is ridiculous. The factory is ridiculous. The explanation is ridiculous. But the problem is not ridiculous at all. It is the oldest problem in the world: who must work, who gets to decide, and how long a system can survive by calling coercion a workflow.
